To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mean velocity dispersion of the maxBCC galaxy clusters increases with richness from 202 ±10 to more than 850 ±100 km s-1 and that the velocity dispersion has a scatter of at most 40% ±3.5%.
the velocity dispersion of a galaxy cluster increases with richness, and the scatter in the velocity dispersion at fixed optical richness is small.
the velocity dispersion–richness relation has a mean that increases from 202 km s-1 to 854 km s-1 with richness and a scatter that is at most 40%, declining to 15% for rich clusters.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the BCG-galaxies velocity correlation function, the scatter of the velocity correlation function at fixed richness, and the velocity dispersion function.
the study of the velocity dispersion function, the scatter in this function, and the velocity dispersion–richness relation, and its implications for the mass–richness relation.
the distribution of galaxies in the velocity space around the centers of clusters.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have demonstrated that the velocity dispersion of galaxy clusters can be determined with high accuracy from the richness alone.
the mean and scatter of velocity dispersion at fixed optical richness is measured to within a factor of 2 and a factor of 1.5, respectively, for the maxBCG clusters.
the maxBCG catalog is a robust tool for studying the velocity distribution of galaxy clusters, and the scatter in velocity at fixed richness is low.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the velocity dispersion–richness relation has a low scatter, and thus is useful for constraining cosmological parameters.

we have measured the velocity dispersion function for a sample of 13,000 clusters with 200 < σ < 900 km s-1 and 13 < λ < 200, with the mean and scatter of velocity dispersion at fixed optical richness.
we have measured the mean and scatter of velocity dispersion for galaxy clusters at fixed richness, and have used this information to infer the velocity dispersion function for maxBCG clusters.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the velocity dispersion function for maxBCG clusters has a shape that is consistent with a mass function derived from simulations, but with a normalization that is lower than expected from simulations by a factor of 0.5-0.6, and that the mean velocity dispersion at fixed maxBCG richness is consistent with the mean velocity dispersion expected from simulations.
the velocity dispersion of a galaxy cluster is a good indicator of its total mass.
galaxy clusters are not just a function of richness, but of the richness and velocity dispersion, which together form an excellent observable proxy for cluster mass.
